newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Thomson-CSF shares dive after selloff halt.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Thomson-CSF shares dive after selloff halt.

text.p: Shares in Europe's top defence electronics supplier Thomson-CSF tumbled sharply on Tuesday as investors expressed doubts about the company's future after the government decided to halt its privatisation.

Recently elected Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin cancelled the privatisation planned by his centre-right predecessors on Friday, saying it did not protect the interests of the state, the company or its employees.
Shares in 58-percent state-owned Thomson-CSF fell almost six percent in the market's first reaction following a long weekend.
In early afternoon trading they were 9.6 francs down from Friday at 160 francs, though well above a 1997 low of 144.2.
Shares in missiles maker Lagardere, seen as the loser in a defence sector restructuring favouring a national French solution, dropped 2.91 percent to 173.8 francs.
But engineering firm Alcatel Alsthom, which had bid against Lagardere in the just-cancelled privatisation, rose by just over one percent to 773 francs.
The stock was buoyed by weekend reports that despite halting the selloff, the government would link Alcatel to Thomson-CSF as a minority partner in a restructured French defence giant.
The government said on Friday it would maintain a "decisive" stake in Thomson-CSF in a new plan to be launched soon, but repeated on Tuesday that no decisions had been taken.
"No choice has been made regarding Thomson, as far as the operator itself is concerned nor as far as alliances to be made are concerned," a spokesman for Jospin said.

The share price moves reflected a feeling widespread among analysts that despite the government's stated wish to build European alliances, its first priority was a short-term defence of national sovereignty and jobs.
The move was condemned by defence sector analysts, who said it showed Jospin and his team had fundamentally misunderstood the dynamics of the fast-moving global defence industry.
They added the decision could lead to the long-term decline of an already less robust French industry, squeezed by falling defence budgets and a series of U.S. mega-mergers.

"Industrially and financially we don't really understand the logic of this," said Emmanuel Dubois-Pelerin, analyst with Standard & Poor's in Paris. "They are favouring national and short term interests rather than industrial and long term interests. They think they can combine these two and I'm not sure they perceive the contradictions."
Analysts from outside France were even harsher.

"You can't overstate the problems this is going to cause. This is a demonstration that the French are not interested in restructuring the European defence sector on commercial grounds," said Paul Beaver of Jane's Defence Weekly.
The analysts said a future French defence combine could face problems forging alliances with private companies in the rest of Europe if the government were seen to have too much control.

"The biggest obstacle the government has put in the way of CSF becoming a major and efficient player in the world industry is maintaining their presence in the company's capital," Dubois-Pelerin said.
The government has not said what it means by its decision to keep a decisive stake in Thomson-CSF, but has indicated it will keep a significant chunk of the company's equity in state hands.

Dubois-Pelerin said building a French defence giant from a combination of Thomson-CSF, Alcatel, warplane maker Dassault Aviation and state-owned plane maker Aerospatiale -- one possibility for an internal restructuring -- would result in an "extremely awkward" share structure.
He said this was exactly the sort of thing the European industry was struggling to overcome in the face of the United States' nimble defence giants.
"It doesn't eliminate the likelihood that something big will get done in the European industry but it adds a complicating factor," Dubois-Pelerin said.
